title: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping Opens Friday — With a $100 Million Weekend in Its Sights
excerpt: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opens Friday in theaters and IMAX, with early reviews at 74% on Rotten Tomatoes and tracking toward a $100 million-plus debut.
content:
Panem is back on the big screen. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opens Friday, November 20, in theaters and IMAX, the sixth film in the franchise and its second prequel — and the box office is already watching it like a frontrunner. Early-access screenings began Wednesday night, November 18, and advance ticket sales are running ahead of Wicked's pace.

The film adapts Suzanne Collins's 2025 novel of the same name. Set 24 years before Katniss Everdeen's story, it follows 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy, played by newcomer Joseph Zada, through the 50th Hunger Games — the second Quarter Quell. Francis Lawrence directs, his fifth Hunger Games film. The cast around Zada includes Whitney Peak as Lenore Dove Baird, Mckenna Grace as Maysilee Donner, Ralph Fiennes as President Snow, Jesse Plemons as Plutarch Heavensbee, Elle Fanning as Effie Trinket, Kieran Culkin as Caesar Flickerman, Glenn Close as Drusilla Sickle, Maya Hawke as Wiress, and Kelvin Harrison Jr. as Beetee Latier. Woody Harrelson returns as the older Haymitch.

What the reviews say

Early reviews put the film at 74% on Rotten Tomatoes from more than 100 reviews as of Thursday morning, the third-best score in the franchise behind Catching Fire at 90% and the original at 85%. The film runs 2 hours and 38 minutes and is rated PG-13.

How big could the opening be?

Deadline projects a domestic opening of $90 million to $120 million and a worldwide debut of $160 million to $190 million. Lionsgate itself is projecting a more cautious $85 million domestic opening in about 3,900 theaters, while exhibitors see a path as high as $125 million, and Boxoffice Pro's forecasting panel has it at $100 million to $120 million. The film opens in 84 countries. If it clears $100 million domestically, it would be Lionsgate's first $100 million opener since Mockingjay – Part 2 in 2015, which debuted to $102.7 million.

The stakes are high: the film reportedly cost roughly $185 million to $200 million, making it Lionsgate's most expensive production ever, with a break-even point reported at around $500 million. Presales opened October 28, and one independent tracker has called a $100 million-plus opening a virtual lock.

A 13-year-old's painting opens every UK screening

One of the week's quieter stories: 13-year-old Freja Brown beat more than 1,000 entries to design the official ratings card for the film, and her painting will open every screening of Sunrise on the Reaping in the United Kingdom. She met the cast in London.

What it means

Analysis: Lionsgate is betting that a story whose ending audiences already know can still fill theaters — and the tracking says it can. The draw is not whether Haymitch survives; it is how he becomes the broken mentor audiences met in the original films. The risk is the budget: at roughly $200 million, a merely strong opening is not enough, and the film needs the kind of legs the franchise's best entries had. For now, the numbers point to the biggest Hunger Games opening in more than a decade — and a franchise that, eleven years after Mockingjay, still knows how to pack an arena.
